title: Treasure in the Name
hookLine: the Name is a treasure found within, not in markets (Anand)

lines: A MUSK DEER CHASING A SCENT.
cards: An old Indian story tells of a musk deer. A sweet, wonderful scent follows it everywhere, and it drives the deer wild.
It runs through forests and over hills, nose to every flower and bush, desperate to find where the smell is coming from. It never does, because the scent is coming from the deer itself.
It has been carrying the treasure the whole time it's been searching. Sikh teachers tell it too, and it fits today's theme in Anand Sahib.

teach.b: Anand Sahib, like much of gurbani, speaks of the Name as a treasure, one that can't be found in markets or bought with money, and, as day three hundred eighty-eight said, can't be won by cleverness either.
It's found within, through the Guru. That idea runs right through the Guru Granth Sahib. The Bhagat Pipa, one of the saints whose words sit in the Granth beside the Gurus, put it in one line.

teach.h: WHAT'S IN THE UNIVERSE IS IN THE BODY.
teach.b: In paraphrase: whatever is in the universe is also in the body, and whoever searches, finds it. So the treasure isn't hidden far away. It's hidden close, which is exactly why it's hard to find.
People look outward by habit: markets, achievements, other people's approval, the next place, the next thing. Like the deer, nose-down in every bush but its own. A careful note.
Sikh teaching doesn't call the outer world worthless. It honors the householder: honest work, family, a life lived among people.

teach.h: WORK AND MARKETS AREN'T THE ENEMY.
teach.b: Work and markets aren't the enemy; the point is where the treasure is kept. You can work at the market all day. You just won't find the Name for sale there.
And how do you look within?

teach.h: SIMRAN, SHABAD, SANGAT: A LAMP INWARD.
teach.b: The Sikh answer is simple and steady: simran, remembering the Name; the shabad, the Guru's Word; and the sangat, the company of others on the same path. Together they're like a lamp turned inward.
And like the deer's musk, the treasure was carried along the whole time the searching went on.

how: Many Sikhs understand the Name as a treasure found within through simran, the Guru's Word and the sangat, a theme that runs through Anand Sahib and the whole Guru Granth Sahib.

o: a treasure, found within, not for sale
a temple built to hold sacred texts
a prize won in a market lottery

p: searched for a scent that was its own
what's in the universe is in the body
where the Name isn't for sale

s: in Sikh teaching, work and markets are the enemy
Sikh teaching honors honest work and family life. the Name just isn't for sale in the market.
the Guru Granth Sahib includes the words of Bhagat Pipa
a saint whose line says what's in the universe is in the body, and the searcher finds it.
the treasure, in this picture, is hidden somewhere far away
it's hidden close, within, which is why it's easy to miss.

games.q: you're the musk deer, running from hill to hill after a wonderful scent you can never find. what's the answer the story gives?
o: the scent is your own: the treasure is within.
give up on the scent entirely.
games.why: the musk was in the deer's own body the whole time. Sikh teachers use the story for the Name: a treasure found within, through the Guru.

practice: Close or lower your eyes and breathe slowly; instead of following your thoughts outward to the day's plans and people, turn your attention gently toward the place it's coming from: the breath, the stillness under the thoughts.
Don't try to find anything; just look in, the way you'd look into a quiet room. If you pray, let Waheguru, said softly, lead you in; if not, rest in the looking.

wordCard.voice: Nidhaan, treasure. Anand's picture of the Name as a nidhaan found within, through the Guru, not bought in any market, like the musk deer's own scent.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nidhaan, treasure; gurbani often calls the Name a treasure found within.

carryVoice: Your line: treasure within. The deer never needed a map, only a turn of the head. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anand Sahib, Ang 917–922 (the Name as treasure within)
Bhagat Pipa, Raag Dhanasari, Ang 695 ('jo brahmande soee pinde, jo khojai so paavai')
